title: Medical Microbiology and Parasitology (Clinical)
description: Host–microbe interactions, major bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic infections in Nigeria, and principles of laboratory diagnosis and infection control.

topics.title: Host–Parasite Relationships and Immunity to Infection
topics.summary: Virulence factors, innate and adaptive immunity, vaccines and immunisation principles.

notes.b: Pathogenicity is the ability to cause disease; virulence is its degree. Virulence factors: adhesins and pili (colonisation), capsules (resist phagocytosis — pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Klebsiella), invasins, enzymes (hyaluronidase, coagulase, IgA protease), exotoxins (proteins secreted mainly by Gram-positives — tetanus, diphtheria, botulinum, cholera toxins; toxoids used as vaccines) and endotoxin (lipid A of Gram-negative LPS — fever, septic shock, DIC). Koch's postulates link microbes to disease. Normal flora protect by colonisation resistance; antibiotics disrupt it (e.g. C. difficile, candidiasis).

Innate immunity (skin, mucous membranes, complement, phagocytes, NK cells, fever, interferons) is rapid and non-specific; adaptive immunity (B cells/antibodies — humoral; T cells — cell-mediated) is specific with memory. IgM is the first antibody in a primary response (indicates recent infection); IgG predominates in secondary responses and crosses the placenta; IgA protects mucosal surfaces and is in breast milk; IgE mediates allergy and anti-helminth responses. Active immunity follows infection or vaccination (live attenuated — BCG, measles, yellow fever, oral polio; inactivated — IPV; toxoids — tetanus, diphtheria; subunit/recombinant — hepatitis B, HPV; conjugate — Hib, pneumococcal, MenA). Passive immunity: maternal antibodies, immunoglobulins and antitoxins (e.g. tetanus immunoglobulin, rabies immunoglobulin).
k: Live vaccines: BCG, measles, yellow fever, OPV

topics.title: Important Bacterial Infections in Nigeria
topics.summary: Tuberculosis, typhoid, meningitis, cholera, tetanus, diphtheria and STIs.

notes.b: Nigeria has one of the highest TB burdens globally. TB is spread by airborne droplet nuclei; symptoms include cough for 2 weeks or more, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Diagnosis: GeneXpert MTB/RIF, sputum smear microscopy, culture, chest X-ray; TB–HIV co-infection is common. Treatment: 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (2RHZE) followed by 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid (4RH) under DOTS; multidrug-resistant TB needs second-line regimens. Typhoid (enteric) fever from Salmonella Typhi (faecal–oral) causes step-ladder fever, abdominal pain, relative bradycardia and, rarely, rose spots; complications include intestinal perforation (typically terminal ileum, second–third week). Diagnosis by blood culture; the Widal test is unreliable and over-used in Nigeria. Treatment depends on susceptibility (ceftriaxone, azithromycin, fluoroquinolones in susceptible strains).

Cerebrospinal (meningococcal) meningitis epidemics occur in the dry season in the northern 'meningitis belt' (serogroups A, C, W, X; MenAfriVac and MenFive conjugate vaccines); features include fever, headache, neck stiffness and a petechial rash; ceftriaxone is first-line. Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) causes profuse 'rice-water' diarrhoea and rapid dehydration — rehydration (ORS, IV Ringer's lactate) is the cornerstone, with antibiotics (doxycycline, azithromycin) as adjuncts. Neonatal tetanus follows unhygienic cord care; prevention by maternal tetanus–diphtheria vaccination and clean delivery. Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) causes a grey adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane and 'bull neck' — recent outbreaks in Nigeria reflect low vaccination coverage; treat with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics. Gonorrhoea, syphilis (VDRL/RPR screening, treated with benzathine penicillin) and chlamydia are common sexually transmitted infections.
k: Neonatal tetanus: clean cord care + maternal vaccination

topics.title: Viral Infections: HIV, Hepatitis and Viral Haemorrhagic Fevers
topics.summary: HIV diagnosis and ART, hepatitis B and C, Lassa fever, yellow fever and measles.

notes.b: HIV (a retrovirus) infects CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells via CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors. Transmission: sexual, blood, and mother-to-child (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding). Diagnosis in Nigeria uses a serial rapid-test algorithm (screening test, confirmatory test, tie-breaker); infants under 18 months need virological (PCR/DNA) testing because of maternal antibodies. All people with HIV should start antiretroviral therapy (treat all), with first-line tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD); monitor with viral load ('Undetectable = Untransmittable'). Opportunistic infections: TB (commonest cause of death), Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi sarcoma, oral candidiasis; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Hepatitis B (DNA virus) is highly endemic in Nigeria — HBsAg indicates infection, anti-HBs immunity, HBeAg high infectivity, anti-HBc (IgM) acute infection; vaccination at birth prevents mother-to-child transmission. Hepatitis C is curable with direct-acting antivirals.

Lassa fever (arenavirus; reservoir Mastomys natalensis rats) is endemic in Nigeria, peaking in the dry season (December–April); transmission via rodent excreta and person-to-person in hospitals. It presents with fever, malaise, sore throat, vomiting, facial oedema, bleeding and hearing loss; diagnosis by RT-PCR (at designated labs); treated with ribavirin (most effective when started early), supportive care and strict infection prevention and control; case fatality among confirmed cases is often around 15–20%. Yellow fever (flavivirus, Aedes mosquitoes) causes fever, jaundice and haemorrhage; prevented by a single dose of vaccine (lifelong protection). Ebola (filovirus) had one imported outbreak in Lagos (2014), contained by contact tracing. Measles (paramyxovirus, highly contagious) causes fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a maculopapular rash; complications include pneumonia, diarrhoea, encephalitis and blindness (vitamin A deficiency) — give vitamin A to all children with measles.
k: Measles: Koplik spots; give vitamin A

topics.title: Malaria and Other Protozoal Infections
topics.summary: Malaria life cycle, diagnosis and treatment; trypanosomiasis, leishmaniasis, amoebiasis and toxoplasmosis.

notes.b: Nigeria carries the world's largest share of the global malaria burden. Plasmodium falciparum causes most cases (also P. malariae, P. ovale, P. vivax rarely). The female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites, which infect hepatocytes (exo-erythrocytic stage), releasing merozoites that invade red cells (erythrocytic cycle — ring forms, trophozoites, schizonts) causing fever; some form gametocytes taken up by mosquitoes (sexual cycle). P. vivax and ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites causing relapses. Diagnosis: microscopy of thick (detection) and thin (species, parasite density) Giemsa-stained films, or rapid diagnostic tests (HRP2 for falciparum). Severe malaria (impaired consciousness/cerebral malaria, convulsions, severe anaemia, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, jaundice, haemoglobinuria, shock, hyperparasitaemia) requires IV/IM artesunate; uncomplicated malaria is treated with ACTs (artemether–lumefantrine first line). Prevention: LLINs, IPTp with SP, seasonal malaria chemoprevention, the RTS,S and R21 vaccines.
k: Thick film: detection; thin film: species

notes.b: Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness; T. brucei gambiense in West Africa, tsetse fly) progresses from a haemolymphatic stage (Winterbottom's sign — posterior cervical lymphadenopathy) to a meningoencephalitic stage with sleep disturbance. Leishmaniasis (sandfly) causes cutaneous ulcers or visceral disease (kala-azar — fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia). Amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica) causes dysentery with flask-shaped ulcers and amoebic liver abscess ('anchovy sauce' pus), treated with metronidazole plus a luminal agent. Giardiasis causes malabsorption. Toxoplasmosis (cat faeces, undercooked meat) is dangerous in pregnancy (congenital infection — chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification) and in AIDS (ring-enhancing brain lesions). Cryptosporidium causes chronic diarrhoea in AIDS.
k: Amoebic liver abscess: anchovy sauce pus

topics.title: Helminths and Fungal Infections
topics.summary: Soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis, filariasis, onchocerciasis, and superficial and systemic mycoses.

notes.b: Soil-transmitted helminths: Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm — intestinal obstruction, Loeffler's pneumonitis), hookworm (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale — skin penetration, iron deficiency anaemia), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm — rectal prolapse) and Strongyloides (autoinfection, hyperinfection in immunosuppression); treated with albendazole or mebendazole (ivermectin for Strongyloides). Schistosomiasis: S. haematobium (urinary — terminal haematuria, bladder calcification and cancer; eggs with terminal spine in urine) and S. mansoni (intestinal/hepatic — periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension; lateral spine in stool); praziquantel treatment. Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti — Culex/Anopheles; elephantiasis, hydrocele; night blood films) and onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus — Simulium blackflies near fast rivers; skin nodules, itching, 'leopard skin', river blindness; skin snips) are targeted by mass drug administration with ivermectin and albendazole. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) causes cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis — a cause of epilepsy. Guinea worm is nearly eradicated in Nigeria.

Superficial mycoses: dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) cause tinea capitis (common in Nigerian children), tinea corporis, pedis and cruris; pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia) causes hypo- or hyperpigmented patches. Diagnosis: skin scrapings in 10–20% KOH, culture on Sabouraud agar. Subcutaneous: mycetoma (Madura foot — chronic swelling with sinuses discharging grains, common in northern Nigeria). Systemic/opportunistic: Candida (oral thrush, oesophageal candidiasis in AIDS, vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy and diabetes), Cryptococcus neoformans (meningitis in AIDS — India ink, cryptococcal antigen; treated with amphotericin B and flucytosine then fluconazole), Pneumocystis jirovecii (pneumonia in AIDS — cotrimoxazole), Histoplasma (including African histoplasmosis — H. capsulatum var. duboisii), and Aspergillus.
